QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality–Diversity

Takashi Ishida Affiliation: Sakana AI    Taro Makino Affiliation: Sakana AI    Issa Sugiura Affiliation: Sakana AI
Abstract

Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target, comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. We formalize open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together with a hypothesis, a natural-language reason why the item fits the needs of a decision maker. We propose QD-Rec, a quality–diversity method that selects items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses with a foundation model from earlier ones kept in an archive as stepping stones. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings.

  Code: github.com/SakanaAI/QD-Rec

1 Introduction

Open-ended search continually produces novel and increasingly capable or diverse discoveries, and each can serve as a stepping stone for further discovery (Stanley and Lehman, 2015; Hughes et al., 2024). Foundation models can act as the generator in this search, drawing on earlier candidates to write new ones. This approach has found candidates that no single query to the model would produce, including creative text (Bradley et al., 2024), adversarial prompts for red teaming (Samvelyan et al., 2024), tasks that reveal a model’s capabilities (Lu et al., 2025), loss functions (Lu et al., 2024), faster algorithms (Novikov et al., 2025), new mathematical constructions (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025), agent designs (Hu et al., 2025), and self-improving agents (Zhang et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b).

We ask whether open-ended search can extend to recommendation for decision-making. Unlike open-ended generation, where the model generates new candidates, many decisions are choices from a fixed pool of candidates: an acquirer chooses among the companies that exist, a reader among the papers already written, a marketer among the customers. At first glance, this leaves no room for open-endedness, since the pool is finite and known in advance. However, only the items are fixed. The same item can be chosen for many different reasons, so the search over reasons is still open-ended.

We therefore treat recommendation for such decisions as an open-ended search over item–hypothesis pairs. A hypothesis is a natural-language explanation of why an item fits the decision maker’s profile, such as the profile of one acquirer or one reader. The search returns a diverse, high-quality set of such pairs for a single profile, rather than one ranked list of items. We call this problem open-ended recommendation. In high-stakes decisions, people need to compare candidate items together with the reasons for choosing them (Aggarwal, 2016). We evaluate the set by its quality and diversity, following the quality–diversity (QD) view of illuminating a space of alternatives (Mouret and Clune, 2015).

Open-ended recommendation has two properties that make open-ended search a good fit. First, evaluation is costly: we learn a recommendation’s value only by writing its hypothesis and judging it, so we cannot simply score every possible recommendation in advance and sort them. The system must therefore decide which item to evaluate next and learn from each result. Second, the space is larger than the pool: each item allows unlimited hypotheses, so even evaluating every item once would leave most of the space unexplored. Good hypotheses often come from adapting or combining earlier ones, so keeping modest intermediate hypotheses as stepping stones can help (Lehman and Stanley, 2011; Stanley and Lehman, 2015). QD and novelty search were designed for such problems (Risi et al., 2025), but to our knowledge they have not been applied to recommendation.11 1 Evolutionary methods have been applied to decision-making more broadly, for example to evolve neural networks that prescribe interventions against COVID-19 (Risi et al., 2025, Section 6.4).

We introduce QD-Rec, a quality–diversity search method for open-ended recommendation (Figure 1). In QD-Rec, an LLM called the proposer writes hypotheses, and an LLM judge or humans score them. Each iteration has three steps. A contextual bandit selects an item from the candidate pool, balancing items that look promising against regions the archive has not yet covered. The proposer generates a hypothesis for that item, building on a few earlier hypotheses from the archive. The new recommendation is kept if it is novel, or if it is better than its nearest neighbor in the archive. Novelty and quality are thus judged locally, by comparison with nearby recommendations.

Our contributions are: (i) we formalize open-ended recommendation as a quality–diversity search over item–hypothesis pairs, where the items come from a fixed pool; (ii) we propose QD-Rec, with two ablations isolating its components (Table 1); and (iii) across four domains and two proposers, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality in most LLM-judged settings, usually builds the largest archive, and outperforms diversity-aware rerankers on human-rated quality.

2 Background and Related Work

We briefly review quality–diversity methods and novelty search, evolutionary loops built around foundation models, and recommender systems.

Quality–diversity and novelty search.

Quality–diversity (QD) methods aim to discover a set of high-performing yet diverse solutions rather than a single optimum. Multi-dimensional Archive of Phenotypic (MAP) Elites “illuminates” a search space by maintaining an archive and retaining elites across behavioral niches (Mouret and Clune, 2015). Novelty search emphasizes exploration by rewarding behavioral novelty, providing a mechanism for stepping-stone trajectories in which intermediate solutions enable later progress (Lehman and Stanley, 2011). Recent work continues to revisit local competition and novelty definitions in QD, including dominated novelty variants (Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2025), and extensions that reduce dependence on hand-designed behavioral descriptors, such as dimensionless MAP-Elites (Dharna et al., 2025).

Foundation models in evolutionary loops.

A growing family of systems places a frozen large model inside an evolutionary or QD loop as a proposal operator or mutator, keeping an archive of artifacts that the model conditions on to propose the next: diverse creative text in QDAIF (Bradley et al., 2024), adversarial prompts in Rainbow Teaming (Samvelyan et al., 2024), code and program search in ELM (Lehman et al., 2023) and FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), algorithm discovery in AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), sample-efficient program evolution in ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), open-ended evaluation tasks in Automated Capability Discovery (Lu et al., 2025), and agent designs in ADAS (Hu et al., 2025).22 2 In evolutionary loops, foundation models can also play roles other than proposing new artifacts. In CycleQD (Kuroki et al., 2025) and AC/DC (Dai et al., 2026), they are themselves the artifacts being evolved. In a replication of Picbreeder (Earle et al., 2026), vision–language models take the place of its human evaluators. A separate line of work is self-referential: STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024), the Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2026a), the Huxley–Gödel Machine (Wang et al., 2026), and Hyperagents (Zhang et al., 2026b) turn the search on the machinery itself, so the improved scaffold or agent performs the next round of improvement. QD-Rec belongs to the first group, with item–hypothesis pairs as the artifacts. However, these systems create new artifacts, while QD-Rec must choose its items from a fixed pool.

Recommender systems.

Recommenders learn either offline, from a fixed dataset of past interactions (Aggarwal, 2016), or online, as a sequential decision problem with an exploration–exploitation trade-off, usually modeled as a (contextual) bandit (Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020; Agarwal et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Agrawal and Goyal, 2013; Song et al., 2022). The evolutionary loops above are sequential as well, but they generate their candidates rather than choose them from a pool. QD-Rec does both, generating hypotheses for items selected from a fixed pool, so it selects items with a contextual bandit; unlike a recommender’s bandit, however, it is judged, as in QD, by its final archive. Orthogonally, a long line of work treats diversity, novelty, coverage, and serendipity as first-class objectives (McNee et al., 2006; Ziegler et al., 2005; Vargas and Castells, 2011; Kaminskas and Bridge, 2016), pursued offline by re-ranking (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998; Chen et al., 2018) and online by diversity-aware bandits (Radlinski et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2020). These methods diversify the list shown to a user; QD-Rec instead enforces diversity at archive admission, following recent QD systems (Lu et al., 2025; Dharna et al., 2025): an LLM judges whether each new pair is novel relative to its nearest archive neighbors. Finally, explainable recommendation adds a natural-language explanation to each recommended item (Zhang and Chen, 2020), and so do LLM recommenders that reason before choosing or justify afterward. QD-Rec also pairs each item with a reason, but it does so inside an evolutionary loop.

3 Open-Ended Recommendation

Let 𝒞={c1,…,cN}\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{N}\} be a fixed candidate pool (e.g., companies for M&A, customer profiles for targeting, papers, or books), and let π\pi be the profile of one decision maker. A hypothesis h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} is a natural-language explanation of why an item fits π\pi, and the hypothesis space ℋ\mathcal{H} is unbounded. A recommendation is a pair (c,h)∈𝒞×ℋ(c,h)\in\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{H}, so the same item can be recommended several times with different hypotheses. Its quality q⁡(c,h)q(c,h) is a score from a human or an LLM judge, for example on a 0 to 10 scale. The score is known only after the hypothesis is written and evaluated, and each evaluation is costly. Given π\pi and 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the task is to return a set 𝒮⊂𝒞×ℋ\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{H} of recommendations that have high quality and differ from one another, using at most TT evaluations. Section 5.1 defines the metrics for quality and diversity.

4 QD-Rec

We present QD-Rec, an archive-based quality–diversity (QD) method for open-ended recommendation. QD-Rec keeps an archive 𝒜\mathcal{A} of retained recommendations and returns it as 𝒮\mathcal{S} at the end of the run. Each new entry is compared only with its nearest neighbors in the archive to decide whether it is kept. Each archive entry xx stores a recommendation (c,h)(c,h), its embedding e=Embed⁡(c,h)e=\mathrm{Embed}(c,h), and its quality score q⁡(x)q(x). The embedding is computed from a structured item profile followed by the hypothesis text. We use cosine similarity sim⁡(xi,xj)=⟨ei,ej⟩/(‖ei‖​‖ej‖)\mathrm{sim}(x_{i},x_{j})=\langle e_{i},e_{j}\rangle/(\|e_{i}\|\,\|e_{j}\|) to define these neighborhoods.

4.1 Local novelty, ranking, and archive update

At each step we propose a new pair by selecting an item cc and generating a hypothesis hh (Section 4.2); we write xnew=(c,h,enew)x_{\text{new}}=(c,h,e_{\text{new}}) with enew=Embed⁡(c,h)e_{\text{new}}=\mathrm{Embed}(c,h) for the proposed entry (its quality estimate is not yet known at this point). We retrieve the kk nearest neighbors from the archive,

𝒩k​(xnew)=arg​maxx∈𝒜k⁡sim​(xnew,x).\mathcal{N}_{k}(x_{\text{new}})=\operatorname*{arg\,max}^{k}_{x\in\mathcal{A}}\,\mathrm{sim}(x_{\text{new}},x).

The archive update then proceeds in the following two steps:

  • •

    Novelty check: an LLM judge is prompted with the profile π\pi, the new entry, and its kk nearest neighbors, and returns a binary decision is_novel∈{0,1}\texttt{is\_novel}\in\{0,1\} (with brief reasoning). A novel entry is admitted immediately; no comparison is made.

  • •

    Local quality comparison (only when not novel): we use a blind pairwise duel: of the kk neighbors only the single nearest one is contested. It and xnewx_{\text{new}} are shuffled into two anonymous positions, pointwise scores are withheld, and the judge, never told which of the two is the newcomer, chooses the stronger under π\pi (ties are not allowed). If xnewx_{\text{new}} wins it replaces that neighbor; otherwise it is discarded. Algorithm 1 writes this comparison as Betterπ\mathrm{Better}_{\pi}. Separating the two questions keeps the retention comparison blind (the judge cannot favor or disfavor an entry for being new) and skips the comparison call entirely whenever the entry is novel.

This embedding-neighborhood admission scheme is inspired by recent novelty-search/QD systems that use learned representations for similarity and archive admission (Lu et al., 2025; Dharna et al., 2025).

The quality score q⁡(x)q(x) of each evaluated pair (Section 3) has two uses. The bandit reward r⁡(x)r(x) is the score divided by the maximum of its scale, so that rewards lie in [0,1][0,1]. Reported Quality averages the score over the final archive, on its original scale.

4.2 Item selection and hypothesis generation

The archive mechanics above leave two decisions open: which item c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} to evaluate next, and how to generate a hypothesis hh for it.

Item selection.

Each candidate item cc has a precomputed candidate embedding ψ⁡(c)∈ℝd\psi(c)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, distinct from the archive-entry embedding ee and taken to be L2-normalized. It embeds the item’s text: the title and abstract of a paper, the title and description of a book, the business description of a company, or the profile of a customer. We model a scalar reward r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1] by Bayesian linear regression, r=ψ​(c)⊤​θ+ϵr=\psi(c)^{\top}\theta+\epsilon with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) and prior θ∼𝒩⁡(0,λ−1​I)\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{-1}I). For the set 𝒟\mathcal{D} of evaluated pairs we maintain the sufficient statistics

A=λI+σ−2∑(ψ,r)∈𝒟ψψ⊤,b=σ−2∑(ψ,r)∈𝒟rψ,θ∣𝒟∼𝒩(A−1b,A−1),A\;=\;\lambda I+\sigma^{-2}\!\!\sum_{(\psi,r)\in\mathcal{D}}\!\!\psi\psi^{\top},\qquad b\;=\;\sigma^{-2}\!\!\sum_{(\psi,r)\in\mathcal{D}}\!\!r\,\psi,\qquad\theta\mid\mathcal{D}\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}(A^{-1}b,\;A^{-1}),

and a new observation (ψ⁡(c),r)(\psi(c),r) updates them in closed form:

A←A+σ−2​ψ​(c)​ψ​(c)⊤,b←b+σ−2​r​ψ​(c).A\;\leftarrow\;A+\sigma^{-2}\,\psi(c)\psi(c)^{\top},\qquad b\;\leftarrow\;b+\sigma^{-2}\,r\,\psi(c).

Linear Thompson sampling (Agrawal and Goyal, 2013) then draws θ~∼𝒩⁡(A−1​b,A−1)\tilde{\theta}\sim\mathcal{N}(A^{-1}b,A^{-1}) at each step, and, with a small modification for diversity, we select the candidate that maximizes the diversity-aware selection score

s⁡(c)=ψ​(c)⊤​θ~+β​d​(c,ℛ),d⁡(c,ℛ)= 1−maxc′∈ℛ⁡ψ​(c)⊤​ψ​(c′),s(c)\;=\;\psi(c)^{\top}\tilde{\theta}\;+\;\beta\,d(c,\mathcal{R}),\qquad d(c,\mathcal{R})\;=\;1-\max_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\psi(c)^{\top}\psi(c^{\prime}), (1)

where ℛ\mathcal{R} collects the candidate embeddings of the current archive. The bonus d⁡(c,ℛ)d(c,\mathcal{R}) is the cosine distance to the nearest covered item (the standard nearest-neighbor novelty measure), so it is large exactly when nothing similar has been archived yet, and β≥0\beta\geq 0 trades this coverage of under-explored regions against the sampled quality estimate ψ​(c)⊤​θ~\psi(c)^{\top}\tilde{\theta}. The bandit reward is unchanged: after evaluation we update the posterior using the normalized reward r⁡(x)r(x) defined above, so β\beta affects only which items are chosen for evaluation, steering the archive to spread rather than cluster. Setting β=0\beta=0 recovers the plain quality-only bandit; we use β=1\beta=1 throughout. We warm-start the posterior from the seed archive: each seed entry contributes one observation (ψ⁡(c),r⁡(x))(\psi(c),r(x)), using the same normalization.

An item can be selected more than once, because a new hypothesis for it can receive a different quality score. The same item can also appear in the archive several times.33 3 For an item already in the archive, the bonus d⁡(c,ℛ)d(c,\mathcal{R}) is zero, so QD-Rec rarely selects it again. In our runs, no final QD-Rec archive contains the same item twice. If a new hypothesis for an item differs enough from the entries near it, the novelty check admits it as a new entry.

Hypothesis generation (evolutionary operator).

Given the selected item cc, we prompt the proposer LLM with the profile π\pi, the item cc, and mm exemplars sampled uniformly from the current archive. The prompt presents the exemplars as existing hypotheses and instructs the model to apply one of three operators, mutate (adapt one exemplar’s angle to cc), crossover (combine angles from several exemplars), or explore (propose an angle the exemplars miss), so the archive acts as an evolving population (Guo et al., 2024; Lehman et al., 2023).

Simpler variants.

We also define two simpler variants of QD-Rec, which serve as ablations of the full method. Novelty+Evo replaces the bandit with uniform-random item selection. Novelty removes both the bandit and the exemplars, so the proposer generates hypotheses zero-shot. All three methods share the archive update of Section 4.1, and Table 1 compares them. Algorithm 1 gives QD-Rec in full.

4.3 Implementation details

To speed up experiments, we run the loop in parallel batches where workers propose and evaluate candidates against a snapshot of the current archive. To select a batch of BB items, we extend the single-draw rule of Section 4.2: we take BB independent posterior draws θ~1,…,θ~B\tilde{\theta}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\theta}_{B}, and for each θ~i\tilde{\theta}_{i} select the candidate maximizing s⁡(c)s(c) while excluding items already chosen in the batch and adding them to ℛ\mathcal{R}, so the diversity bonus discourages near-duplicates within a batch as well as against the archive. After each batch, we reconcile results by filtering near-duplicate additions (above a cosine-similarity threshold) and resolving replacement collisions (multiple workers targeting the same neighbor). The bandit uses prior precision λ=1\lambda=1 and noise standard deviation σ=0.1\sigma=0.1, the novelty check uses k=3k=3 nearest neighbors, and each run starts from 1010 seed entries.

5 Experiments

We evaluate the three variants (Novelty, Novelty+Evo, QD-Rec; Table 1) across four domains.

5.1 Setup

Common protocol.

Our main experiment uses claude-sonnet-5 as the hypothesis proposer; we additionally report a weaker-proposer ablation that swaps in claude-haiku-4-5. The judge is gpt-5.6-terra in every configuration and domain, a different model family from both proposers, to prevent self-preference bias (Wataoka et al., 2024). Proposer and judge both run with reasoning effort set to high. The weak-proposer ablation model does not support the effort parameter and runs without it or extended thinking. We leave the temperature setting to the provider default for claude-haiku-4-5. Each configuration runs 1,0001{,}000 evaluations (proposal–judge cycles) per method in all four domains, executed in generations of up to 2020 parallel evaluations, with the archive reconciled between generations (Section 4.3). Novelty+Evo and QD-Rec condition each proposal on m=3m=3 archive exemplars. Runs are repeated for five random seeds. Each run begins from a seed archive under the same profile π\pi; the seed controls the pipeline’s own sampling randomness (parent selection, item ordering) while LLM sampling stays at the provider default, so across-seed spread measures the stochasticity of the full pipeline.

We embed archive entries and candidate items with OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small at 512512 output dimensions, L2-normalized, and use cosine similarity for kk-nearest-neighbor retrieval.

Methods.

We evaluate the proposed method QD-Rec and its two ablations (Novelty, Novelty+Evo) under matched evaluation budgets and shared hyperparameters within each domain. Table 1 summarizes the three variants as an “ingredients” view: all share the archive mechanics; Novelty+Evo adds the evolutionary few-shot operator, and QD-Rec additionally adds diversity-aware bandit item selection.

Domains.

We instantiate the framework on four fixed-pool domains, each realizing the hypothesis hh in its native genre. The first, Goodreads, is a grounding check whose quality signal is a real human rating rather than an LLM judge; the other three are heterogeneous applied settings. Full dataset construction (sources, filtering, pool sizes, and the specific profiles used) is in Appendix C.

  • •

    Goodreads. The pool 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the children’s books a reader has rated (Wan and McAuley, 2018); the profile π\pi is that reader (summarized from past reviews); hh is a reading memo on whether they would enjoy a book. Uniquely, quality is not an LLM judge but the reader’s own 11–55 rating, held out of all prompts and used only as the reward and replacement signal (Appendix C), testing whether QD still yields meaningful quality–diversity tradeoffs under a real human signal. This Quality measure evaluates the book for the reader, not the generated memo: changing the memo cannot change the rating, although it can affect novelty and archive geometry.

  • •

    M&A target discovery. 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a universe of 6,332 US companies built from LSEG Workspace data (business descriptions, industry taxonomy, financials). The business descriptions average approximately 123 words. The profile π\pi is an acquirer (Walt Disney or JPMorgan Chase), and hh is an acquisition thesis (e.g. capability acquisition vs. market access vs. vertical integration). Deal sourcing motivates it: teams want a diverse set of strategic theses rather than a single shortlist.

  • •

    Marketing. 𝒞\mathcal{C} is 10,000 synthetic customer profiles from California, sampled from NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA (Meyer and Corneil, 2025). The customer profiles average approximately 685 words. The profile π\pi is a product (a desktop 3D printer or an online upskilling subscription), and hh is a targeting hypothesis explaining why a profile is an attractive target for π\pi, yielding a map of distinct targeting angles rather than a ranked list.

  • •

    Paper-abstract exploration. 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the titles and abstracts of 17,511 papers accepted at ICLR 2026, ICML 2026 and NeurIPS 2025 (Paper Copilot (2026), Jing Yang), π\pi a researcher profile (an open-endedness researcher or an applied researcher at an AI startup), and hh a research memo linking a paper to π\pi. The scale of the AI literature motivates it: researchers need diverse, well-justified reading directions under limited time. Candidate embeddings for bandit item selection are precomputed from title+abstract; archive embeddings are computed from title+abstract+memo.

Evaluation.

Four metrics summarize a run’s final active archive.

  • •

    Quality is the mean pointwise score of its entries: the judge score (0–10), or in Goodreads the reader’s real star rating (1–5).

  • •

    Diversity is one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity between archive-entry embeddings, computed in the original embedding space (the complement of the mean pairwise similarity used to quantify homogenization by Jiang et al., 2025).

  • •

    Coverage is the fraction of occupied cells on a 25×2525{\times}25 grid over a 2D PCA projection (the maps of Figure 2(a)). For each profile, proposer, and trial seed, we fit PCA by full SVD on the union of all three variants’ active archives and use shared axis bounds padded by 1% on each side. Coverage is comparable across methods within that grid; separate profiles, proposers, and seeds use separate grids.

  • •

    Archive size nn is the number of entries that survived admission.

Online evaluation protocol.

We score each recommendation during the search. QD-Rec uses these scores to update its bandit and select subsequent candidates. Final Quality is the mean of the scores already assigned to the recommendations retained in the archive.

5.2 Results

Table 2 reports our main results: mean Quality and semantic Diversity of the three variants (Novelty, Novelty+Evo, QD-Rec) on both profiles of every domain, under both proposers.

Main results.

QD-Rec gives the best mean Quality in most LLM-judged settings (Table 2), often significantly better than both ablations, and it is never significantly worse than the best variant. The gains are largest on M&A. QD-Rec also builds the largest archive in most settings and often has the best MAP-Elites coverage, so its higher Quality does not come from a smaller, more selective archive. Its semantic Diversity is the best or tied for best in every domain except M&A, where it is slightly lower. On Goodreads, where Quality is the reader’s own star rating, the three variants reach similar mean ratings. There, QD-Rec keeps this rating while matching or beating both ablations on archive size, Diversity and coverage.

Cost.

We measure cost as the API spend of a run in US dollars at list prices. It covers every model call: the proposer, the quality judge, the novelty check, the duel, and the embeddings. The three variants make the same calls for each of the 1,0001{,}000 evaluations. They differ only in the proposer prompt, which includes three archive exemplars in Novelty+Evo and QD-Rec, and in how often a duel is needed. The bandit runs locally and adds no API cost. The runs did not log token usage, so we estimate the cost of each call type by re-sending a sample of 840840 archived calls with the same models and settings. We then multiply by the exact number of calls in each run. QD-Rec costs the same as Novelty+Evo, and both cost about 1.3×1.3\times as much as Novelty. More than 90%90\% of the difference comes from the proposer, because the exemplars roughly triple its input. A single run costs between about $13 (Novelty on Goodreads with the claude-haiku-4-5 proposer) and $62 (QD-Rec on Marketing with the claude-sonnet-5 proposer). Goodreads is the cheapest domain because its ratings replace the LLM judge and the duel.

Qualitative maps.

The left column of Figure 2 shows MAP-Elites-style heatmaps for Novelty and QD-Rec on one profile per domain. In each, QD-Rec covers more of the space than Novelty, most visibly for Disney and the 3D printer. Maps for all eight scenarios, including Goodreads and Novelty+Evo, are in Appendix A, and example recommendations are in Appendix E.

Comparison to a no-learning baseline.

To ask whether the online learning and archive machinery earns its cost, we compare against two training-free re-rankers, relevance-MMR (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998) and a quality-weighted DPP with greedy MAP inference (Chen et al., 2018), on Goodreads, where Quality is a real human star rating. Sweeping each baseline’s relevance–diversity weight γ\gamma,no setting of either reaches any QD variant on Quality, and they approach QD-Rec’s semantic Diversity only at their most diversity-favoring settings. The baselines see no ratings while the QD variants query up to 1,0001{,}000, so the gap reflects rating feedback and the archive together, not item selection alone. Full setup and the per-setting table are in Appendix B.

Quality and archive size over the run.

Figures 2(b) and 2(c) plot the current archive’s mean Quality and size nn after every evaluation, replayed from each run’s add/replace/discard history (all eight scenarios in Figure 5). QD-Rec’s Quality keeps rising through the run and ends highest, so its advantage builds up during the run. Archive size nn grows throughout the run as novel hypotheses are added.

Embedding-model sensitivity.

The embedding model defines the novelty neighborhoods, the Diversity metric, the MAP-Elites grid and the bandit’s item features. We therefore re-run one profile per domain with a different embedding model, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B truncated to the same 512512 dimensions (claude-haiku-4-5 proposer, seed 00, one run with batches of 1616 instead of 2020, due to the compute limits of the local machine that runs the embedding model; Table 3). The best variant on Quality and on archive size is the same as with the original embeddings on all four profiles. Diversity is higher for every variant, because the Qwen embeddings are spread more evenly. Diversity and Coverage can therefore be compared only within one embedding space, while the Quality and archive-size orderings are unchanged.

6 Conclusion

We introduced QD-Rec, an archive-based quality–diversity method for open-ended recommendation, where the items are chosen with contextual bandits, and the reasons for recommending them are searched open-endedly. Across four domains, QD-Rec gave the best mean Quality in most settings and usually built the largest archive. As a first work along this line, we kept it relatively simple, and several directions follow.

First, our bandit uses Bayesian linear regression to model reward from fixed item embeddings. Neural contextual bandits (Zhou et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021) could capture nonlinear relationships between these embeddings and reward. More radically, the bandit could be discarded altogether in favor of a coding agent that reads the archive directly, reasons over which regions look exhausted and which look promising, and writes its own selection rule, replacing a fixed parametric reward model with a policy that can be inspected and revised in natural language. Second, exemplars are sampled uniformly from the archive, and could instead be selected by quality, recency, or how often they have already served as exemplars (Earle et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Third, this work focused on the outer loop: which item to evaluate next, and which pairs to retain. The inner hypothesis generator was a single prompted LLM call, and could instead be a full research agent (Shang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026); we kept it lightweight to show that the outer loop is itself a meaningful lever, and expect the two to compose.

Appendix A Additional results: maps and curves over the run for all scenarios

This appendix collects the qualitative maps for all eight scenarios (Figure 3) and the curves over the run, including semantic Diversity, for all eight scenarios (Figure 5), with weaker-proposer (claude-haiku-4-5) counterparts in Figures 4 and 6.

A.1 Qualitative maps: all scenarios

Figure 3 shows the MAP-Elites-style heatmaps of Figure 2(a) for all eight scenarios (both profiles of every domain), each with all three variants. Figure 4 repeats the construction for the weaker-proposer ablation (claude-haiku-4-5).

A.2 Metrics over the run: all scenarios

Figure 5 plots mean Quality, archive size nn, and semantic Diversity against the number of evaluations for all eight scenarios. Figure 6 shows the same curves under the weaker proposer claude-haiku-4-5.

Unlike Quality, Diversity changes little after the first ∼100{\sim}100 evaluations, while archive size nn keeps growing. A likely reason is that admission is decided by the LLM novelty check against nearest neighbors, not by an embedding-distance threshold. New entries then add distinct hypotheses within the region the archive already spans, which raises nn but not the mean pairwise distance.

Appendix B No-learning baselines: relevance-MMR and a quality-weighted DPP

To ask whether the online learning and archive machinery earns its cost, we compare against two training-free re-rankers on Goodreads, where Quality is a real human star rating that neither the learning methods nor the baselines can game. Relevance-MMR (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998) greedily selects items by γcos(item,π)−(1−γ)maxj∈Scos(item,j)\gamma\cos(\text{item},\pi)-(1-\gamma)\max_{j\in S}\cos(\text{item},j) over the same content embeddings, where SS is the set of items selected so far. Quality-weighted DPP (Chen et al., 2018) is the principled counterpart: greedy MAP inference for a determinantal point process maximizing γ​∑i∈Sreli+(1−γ)​log​det(LS)\gamma\sum_{i\in S}\mathrm{rel}_{i}+(1-\gamma)\log\det(L_{S}). Here reli=cos⁡(itemi,π)\mathrm{rel}_{i}=\cos(\text{item}_{i},\pi) is the relevance of item ii, the same relevance MMR uses. The matrix LSL_{S} holds the pairwise cosine similarities of the items in SS, so logdet(LS)\log\det(L_{S}) measures the diversity of the set as its log-volume. In both baselines, the weight γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1] trades relevance against diversity, and γ=1\gamma{=}1 recovers plain top-KK retrieval exactly.

Neither baseline uses an archive, novelty filter, or feedback, and no LLM touches anything that could affect the headline result: selection is pure geometry over precomputed content embeddings, with relevance cos⁡(item,π)\cos(\text{item},\pi) rather than an LLM score (scoring the full pool with an LLM is precisely the cost our setting excludes), and Quality is the human star rating, fixed the moment an item is selected. The only LLM calls are measurement plumbing: after selection, each chosen item receives a zero-shot memo (proposer claude-sonnet-5) and the same joint item+memo embedding the QD entries carry, so that Diversity and Coverage are computed in the same embedding space as Table 2 and every row emits the same item–hypothesis artifact. These memos cannot influence which items are selected or their ratings.

For each reader, the Coverage grid is fitted jointly to all QD, MMR, and DPP rows using full SVD and the same 1% padding convention. This larger reference pool differs from Table 2, so absolute Coverage need not match across tables. The comparison is not a controlled ablation of item selection, however: the QD variants observe the rating of every item they evaluate (up to 1,0001{,}000 per run) and use it for replacement and, in QD-Rec, for the bandit, whereas the baselines see none. They are no-feedback geometric references, and the gap measures what rating feedback and the archive machinery buy together. Every run is matched in archive size nn to the QD-Rec archive of its reader; selection is deterministic given the embeddings, so rows are single runs (Table 4).

No setting of either baseline reaches any QD variant on Quality. The baselines approach QD-Rec’s Diversity only at their most diversity-favoring settings, and a few settings exceed its Coverage. The DPP gives almost the same results as MMR, so the gap is not specific to MMR’s heuristic.

Appendix C Dataset details

This appendix gives the full dataset construction for the four domains of Section 5.1 (sources, filtering, pool sizes, and the specific profiles used).

Goodreads (real human-feedback grounding).

We use the Children subset of the UCSD Goodreads Book Graph (Wan and McAuley, 2018). For each reader, the candidate pool is their own rated books (minus the few used to construct the profile), so every item carries a ground-truth rating. We select two readers by a fixed procedure, set before any experiment. A reader qualifies if they meet six thresholds: at least 200200 rated books, at least 500500 written reviews, a rating standard deviation of at least 0.90.9, at least 70%70\% of shelved books marked as read, at least 80%80\% of sampled reviews in English, and an entropy of at least 2.02.0 nats in their books’ distribution over shelves. Of the 542,145542{,}145 readers, 88 qualify. We take the qualifying reader with the most ratings, and then the one with the most ratings whose most common shelf differs from the first reader’s. This gives a picture-book reader (1,7611{,}761 books) and a series/young-adult reader (1,1171{,}117 books). Goodreads uses the reader’s 11–55 rating in place of the LLM judge, so the bandit reward is q⁡(x)/5q(x)/5. In the local comparison, a new book replaces its nearest neighbor only if its rating is strictly higher; ties keep the incumbent. Books are selected without replacement in all three variants, including seed books and discarded proposals, because a fixed rating means a new memo for the same book would get the same score.

M&A target discovery.

We construct country-specific company universes from LSEG Workspace data that combine (i) tabular financial snapshot features (as of 2024-08-31) and (ii) textual business descriptions. We filter to a target country, retain feature columns with at least 0.80 fill rate, and merge description fields into a single company profile. This yields universes of 6,332 USA companies. The profile π\pi is an acquirer selected from the same universe; in our runs we use two USA acquirers, Walt Disney Co and JPMorgan Chase & Co. For QD-Rec, each candidate company has a precomputed embedding of its business description, used only for bandit item selection. The proposer, the judge and the archive embedding use the full company profile, which also includes the location, the industry classification and the financial features.

Marketing.

We use a subset of the NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA dataset, a large-scale synthetic customer-profile corpus aligned to real-world US demographic distributions (Meyer and Corneil, 2025). We use this synthetic dataset as a proxy in lieu of sensitive real-world customer data. Each customer profile includes demographic attributes (e.g., age, sex, marital status, education, occupation, city/state) and multiple profile facets (professional, sports, arts, travel, culinary). To control for regional heterogeneity we restrict to a single state (California) and sample 10,000 customer profiles for experiments. We use two distinct product profiles (a desktop 3D printer and an online upskilling subscription), spanning different purchase contexts (a one-time tool purchase vs. career reskilling). The seed archive is initialized from sampled customer profiles, and the three variants iteratively generate and evaluate targeting hypotheses for additional profiles.

Paper-abstract exploration.

We use a fixed collection of paper metadata (title and abstract only) drawn from three recent machine-learning conferences: ICLR 2026, ICML 2026, and NeurIPS 2025. We filter to accepted statuses (Oral, Spotlight, and Poster, plus ICLR’s conditional accepts) and retain entries with non-empty identifier, title, and abstract, yielding 17,511 papers (5,358 / 6,341 / 5,812 for ICLR / ICML / NeurIPS respectively). The metadata is obtained from the papercopilot/paperlists repository (Paper Copilot (2026), Jing Yang). We precompute candidate embeddings from title+abstract for bandit item selection. Archive embeddings are computed from the concatenated title, abstract, and memo (item_hypothesis mode) and are used for novelty-neighbor retrieval, semantic Diversity, and Coverage. The three variants generate memos for selected papers and apply the same local novelty-first archive update procedure.

Appendix D Prompt Templates

This appendix lists the prompts used in our experiments. The three variants use the same generation and judging prompts. They differ only in how the next item is selected and whether the generator is shown archive exemplars. For each domain we show the generator prompt, the judge prompt (0–10 score), the novelty-check prompt, and the pairwise-duel prompt, which runs only when an entry is not novel. Goodreads has only the generator and novelty-check prompts, because it uses human ratings for Quality and replacement. Placeholders such as {acquirer_profile} are filled in at run time. A novelty-check or duel response that cannot be parsed never adds an entry to the archive.

D.5 Goodreads-Children (grounding)

Goodreads has no LLM quality judge (Quality is the reader’s held-out star rating), so its prompt set is smaller: memo generation and the novelty check. For a non-novel book, replacement compares its human rating directly with that of its nearest neighbor: a strictly higher rating replaces the neighbor, while a tie or lower rating retains the incumbent. The bandit uses rating/5 for both seed initialization and subsequent updates, while reported Quality remains on the 1–5 scale. Previously tried books, including seeds, are excluded from subsequent selection.

Appendix E Example QD-Rec recommendations

Two QD-Rec recommendations from M&A and marketing (proposer claude-sonnet-5, judge gpt-5.6-terra). Each was made by the mutate operator from a single parent in the archive, and we chose them to show how a parent hypothesis shapes the child. For each, we give the chosen item, the parent hypothesis, the child hypothesis, and the hypothesis that Novelty wrote for the same item without exemplars. Texts are verbatim apart from the replacement of non-ASCII characters.

M&A target discovery: JPMorgan Chase & Co (acquirer)

Acquirer profile: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Hypothesis = acquisition thesis (judge 0–10). QD-Rec run with seed 1; the child is evaluation 312 of 1,000, made by mutate from one parent. Scores: parent 1/10, child 5/10, Novelty 1/10 (seed 2). The child entered the archive and was later replaced by a nearby entry that won a pairwise duel against it.

Novelty wrote its hypothesis for Liberty TripAdvisor without earlier examples. It argued that JPMorgan’s existing Chase Travel platform and commercial partnerships made an acquisition unnecessary, so it offered no affirmative reason to buy the company (1/10). QD-Rec drew on an archived hypothesis proposing that JPMorgan acquire Southwest Airlines. The parent proposed integrating financing, payments and rewards into travel purchases, and using transaction data to improve credit decisions and offer related financial products. The judge recognized this commercial rationale but scored the parent 1/10, citing restrictions on bank ownership of an airline and exposure to fuel, labor and other operating risks.

The mutate operator adapted this rationale to the travel marketplaces described in Liberty TripAdvisor’s company information. The child proposed connecting bookings for activities, dining and accommodation to Chase Travel, rewards redemption and installment financing. It retained the parent’s idea of linking travel purchases to financial services, while changing the target from an airline to a travel platform. The judge rated the child 5/10, although it still raised concerns about competition, acquisition complexity and whether partnerships would suffice. A parent rated only 1/10 thus served as a stepping stone for a more highly rated recommendation about a different company.

In this example, the model generated statements and interpretations absent from the input, including a loyalty base of more than 100 million members. For example, Southwest’s July 22, 2026 announcement came after the model’s knowledge cutoff and reported “nearly 100 million Members.” We could not verify the claim of more than 100 million members. The financial snapshot is dated August 2024, but note that Tripadvisor acquired Liberty TripAdvisor Holdings in April 2025. In this experiment, we supplied the model with only basic financial data and short business descriptions. Using the recommendations for actual decisions would require more detailed and up-to-date information.

Marketing: Upskilling (SkillForge)

Product: SkillForge learning platform. Hypothesis = targeting hypothesis (judge 0–10). QD-Rec run with seed 1; the child is evaluation 438 of 1,000, made by mutate from one parent. Scores: parent 7/10, child 7/10, Novelty 2/10 (seed 3). The child did not enter the archive: it lost the pairwise duel against its nearest archive entry.

Novelty focused on the nurse’s clinical career goals and SkillForge’s lack of accredited nursing courses. It recognized that project management and data analysis could help with his planned screening program, but treated these as peripheral needs and his shift work as an obstacle to study. It concluded that the platform was a poor fit (2/10). QD-Rec drew on an archived hypothesis about a preschool teacher seeking district-wide curriculum leadership. The parent argued that SkillForge could supply project management, data analysis and presentation skills needed for this transition but not fully covered by her teaching training (7/10).

The mutate operator applied this reasoning to the nurse’s ambition to lead a team and launch a community screening program. The child connected project management to coordinating screenings, data analysis to reporting health outcomes, and presentation skills to securing support from hospital administrators or funders. These skills became the main reason to recommend SkillForge as a complement to his clinical education. The child also argued that the platform’s flexible format could suit his irregular schedule. The judge found the connection between his leadership goals and the courses credible and rated the child 7/10. Reusing the teacher’s hypothesis helped QD-Rec connect the nurse’s leadership goals to courses that Novelty had dismissed as peripheral.
